---
title: "Build a local development workflow you can reset in minutes"
date: 2026-04-11
categories: [development]
tags: [local-dev, ddev, direnv, taskfile]
summary: "Learn how to make your local development setup repeatable with containerized services, project-local environment loading, and one-command tasks."
slug: "build-a-local-development-workflow-you-can-reset-in-minutes"
draft: true
---

Ahnii!

If you want a local development workflow that stays predictable across projects and teammates, this post shows you how to combine [DDEV](https://ddev.readthedocs.io/), [direnv](https://direnv.net/), and [Task](https://taskfile.dev/) into one setup you can start, stop, and rebuild without guesswork.

## Prerequisites

- [Git](https://git-scm.com/) installed
- [Docker](https://www.docker.com/) running on your machine
- [DDEV](https://ddev.readthedocs.io/) installed
- [direnv](https://direnv.net/) installed and hooked into your shell
- [Task](https://taskfile.dev/) installed

## Standardize how your project starts

A local workflow breaks down fast when every project uses different commands.

You need one entry point.

For most web projects, that entry point should start services, load environment variables, install dependencies if needed, and tell you what to run next. That sounds simple, but it only stays simple if each tool has one job.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[cd into project] --> B[direnv loads local env]
    B --> C[task setup]
    C --> D[ddev start]
    D --> E[task install]
    E --> F[task dev]
```

This flow keeps your shell setup, containers, and project commands separate. That separation is what makes the workflow easy to repair when one layer fails.

## Use DDEV for project services

You do not want to hand-build database, web server, and cache setup for every repo.

You want the project to declare its services once, then start the same way every time. That is where DDEV helps first.

```yaml
name: sample-app
type: php
docroot: public
php_version: "8.3"
webserver_type: nginx-fpm
router_http_port: "80"
router_https_port: "443"
xdebug_enabled: false
additional_hostnames: []
database:
  type: mariadb
  version: "10.11"
use_dns_when_possible: true
```

This `config.yaml` gives your project a repeatable service definition. You are no longer depending on memory or a README that drifted six months ago.

Once that file exists, your baseline commands stay short.

```bash
ddev start
ddev describe
```

`ddev start` brings the project services up. `ddev describe` shows the local URLs and service details so you can confirm the environment came up the way you expected.

## Load project variables with direnv

You should not keep copying `.env` values into your shell session by hand.

That creates subtle failures. One terminal has the right values. Another does not. The next section only works if you fix that first.

```bash
export APP_ENV=local
export APP_URL=https://sample-app.ddev.site
export DATABASE_URL=mysql://db:db@db:3306/db
export NODE_ENV=development
```

Put values like these in `.envrc`, then allow them once with the shell command below.

```bash
direnv allow
```

`direnv allow` tells direnv to trust the project-local environment file. After that, entering the directory loads the values automatically, and leaving it unloads them.

## Give yourself one command for common tasks

Starting containers is not the same as preparing the app.

You still need commands for dependency install, database setup, tests, and frontend work. If you leave those as tribal knowledge, your workflow is still fragile.

```yaml
version: '3'

tasks:
  setup:
    cmds:
      - ddev start
      - task install

  install:
    cmds:
      - ddev exec composer install
      - ddev exec php artisan migrate
      - ddev exec npm install

  dev:
    cmds:
      - ddev exec npm run dev

  test:
    cmds:
      - ddev exec php artisan test
```

This `Taskfile.yml` gives your project named entry points instead of loose commands in chat threads or old docs. You can hand the repo to someone else and say `task setup`, which is the point.

## Keep container commands inside the project boundary

You will save yourself trouble if you run app commands through DDEV instead of directly on your host machine.

That keeps PHP, Node, and database access tied to the same project context.

```bash
ddev exec php artisan queue:work
ddev exec npm run build
ddev exec php artisan test
```

These commands run inside the project container, not against whatever runtime happens to be installed globally on your laptop. That reduces “works on my machine” failures because the machine matters less.

## Verify the workflow before you trust it

A workflow is only useful if you can destroy it and recover quickly.

Test that on purpose.

```bash
ddev restart
direnv reload
task test
```

These commands check the three layers separately: services, environment loading, and project behavior. If one fails, you know which boundary to inspect instead of debugging everything at once.

You should also test the new-developer path.

```bash
git clone your-repo-url
cd your-repo
direnv allow
task setup
```

This is the shortest path a teammate should need. If these four lines do not work, your workflow still depends on undocumented knowledge.

## Fix the most common local workflow drift

Most local setup problems are not complicated.

They come from one layer changing while the others stay stale.

### Rebuild services when containers drift

```bash
ddev poweroff
ddev start
```

Use this when ports, containers, or network state get weird across projects. It clears DDEV-managed services, then brings the current project back cleanly.

### Reload variables when `.envrc` changes

```bash
direnv allow
direnv reload
```

Use this after editing `.envrc`. It re-approves the file if needed, then refreshes your current shell with the latest project values.

### Reinstall dependencies when the lockfile changes

```bash
task install
```

Run your install task again instead of piecing together half the dependency steps by hand. That only works if your install task is complete, which is why it is worth maintaining.

## Make your README point to the workflow

Your README does not need to teach every command.

It needs to point to the safe path.

```markdown
## Local development

1. Install Docker, DDEV, direnv, and Task.
2. Run `direnv allow` inside the project.
3. Run `task setup`.
4. Run `task dev` to start the frontend watcher.
5. Run `task test` before you commit.
```

This gives readers a short, stable path into the project. The detailed logic lives in your config files, where you can version it and keep it honest.

# Project Name

You use this repository to install the project, run it locally, and build on a clean starting point.

## Install the Project

Clone the repository with [Git](https://git-scm.com/), then install dependencies with [npm](https://www.npmjs.com/) on top of [Node.js](https://nodejs.org/).

```bash
git clone https://github.com/your-org/your-repo.git
cd your-repo
npm install
```

This downloads the code and installs the packages the project needs. Run these commands once before you start local development.

## Run the Project Locally

Start the development server from the project root.

```bash
npm run dev
```

This starts the local app in watch mode. You use it while you write code and check changes in the browser or terminal.

## Build a Production Version

Create a production build before you deploy or test the final output.

```bash
npm run build
```

This compiles the project into deployable assets. Run it when you need to confirm the app builds cleanly outside development mode.

## Use the Main Entry Point

Import the package into your own code when you want to use its primary API.

```js
import { createApp } from './src/index.js';

const app = createApp();
app.start();
```

This shows the smallest useful integration. Replace the import path and startup call with the entry point this repository exposes.
